slides.title: Chapter 11: Comparison Theory
slides.notes: Frame the whole chapter with one sentence: bound the curvature, and the geometry is trapped between the same bound applied to a constant-curvature model space. Everything downstream is a way of making that slogan rigorous. The technical engine is the second variation of arc length, repackaged first as Jacobi fields, then as a Riccati equation for the shape operator of geodesic spheres. The model spaces are the sphere of curvature kappa, Euclidean space, and hyperbolic space, with constant-curvature Jacobi fields s-kappa and c-kappa.

slides.title: The Comparison Principle
slides.notes: This is the conceptual spine. Comparison theorems never compute the geometry of the unknown manifold directly; they sandwich it between space forms of constant curvature kappa whose Jacobi fields are explicit. Stress the asymmetry students confuse: a curvature upper bound gives a lower bound on geodesic spreading and conjugate distance, while a lower bound reverses it. Foreshadow that volume needs only a Ricci lower bound.

slides.title: The Hessian of the Distance Function
slides.notes: The distance function is the right object because its level sets are geodesic spheres and its gradient is the unit radial field. The Hessian of r on directions tangent to a geodesic sphere is exactly the shape operator of that sphere. Its trace is the Laplacian of r, the mean curvature, which returns in volume and Laplacian comparison. Note r is smooth away from p and the cut locus.

slides.title: The Riccati Equation for the Shape Operator
slides.notes: The technical heart. The shape operator satisfies S-prime plus S-squared plus R equals zero along the radial geodesic, with curvature as forcing term. Increasing R pushes S down, so spheres bend less and grow slower. The scalar trace gives an equation in the Laplacian of r forced by Ricci, which is why Ricci alone suffices for volume and Laplacian statements. In constant curvature, S equals c-kappa over s-kappa times the identity.

slides.title: Jacobi Fields and the Rauch Comparison
slides.notes: Jacobi fields linearize the geodesic flow and solve the Jacobi equation with curvature as coefficient. A Jacobi field vanishing at p has logarithmic derivative satisfying the same Riccati equation as the shape operator. Rauch is a Sturm comparison: smaller curvature means faster growth, more spreading, later conjugate points. Rauch is sharp only up to the first conjugate point.

slides.title: Sectional Curvature Comparison
slides.notes: Collects the two halves of Rauch into a dictionary. An upper bound: geodesics spread at least as fast, conjugate points pushed out, exponential map nonsingular longer (route to Cartan-Hadamard). A lower bound: spreading suppressed, conjugate points early, triangles fatten, diameters shrink (feeds Bonnet-Myers). The sign mechanism: curvature is the negative coefficient in the Jacobi equation, so raising it damps growth.

slides.title: Ricci Lower Bound and Bishop-Gromov Volume Comparison
slides.notes: Bishop-Gromov is the volume incarnation of the Riccati trace. Only a Ricci lower bound is needed because the volume density in geodesic polar coordinates has logarithmic derivative equal to the Laplacian of r, forced by radial Ricci. The Riccati comparison bounds that mean curvature above, so volume grows no faster than the space form. The Gromov statement is monotonicity of the ball-volume ratio, the workhorse for precompactness and rigidity.

slides.title: Diameter Bound: Bonnet-Myers as Comparison
slides.notes: Bonnet-Myers is the diameter comparison theorem. The proof is second-variation: a sinusoidal index-form variation plus positive Ricci forces the index form negative once length exceeds pi over root kappa, so the geodesic stops minimizing. Hence bounded diameter, compactness via Hopf-Rinow, and finite fundamental group. The bound equals the round sphere's diameter, and equality is rigidity returning the sphere.

slides.title: Laplacian Comparison
slides.notes: The analytic distillation. The Laplacian of distance is the mean curvature of geodesic spheres, evolving by the scalar Riccati equation; Cauchy-Schwarz controls the nonlinear term and Ricci is the forcing, so Sturm comparison bounds Delta r above by the model value. Regularity caveat: r fails to be smooth on the cut locus, so the inequality is in the barrier/distributional sense, and the singularities only help because Delta r jumps down. Gateway to most Ricci-lower-bound geometry.

slides.title: What Comparison Theory Delivers
slides.notes: Collapse the chapter to one engine, two inputs, three outputs. The engine is the Riccati equation with curvature as forcing; matrix version for sectional/Rauch, scalar trace for Ricci/Bishop-Gromov/Laplacian. Two inputs: sectional bounds and Ricci lower bounds. Three outputs: conjugate-point, volume, and diameter control. Diagnostic question: identify the curvature hypothesis and direction, the governing ODE, and the model space giving the sharp constant.
